opus-5.5.text:
I think you have to be careful about what "slowing down" actually means, because it depends a lot on how you measure it.

If you look at static benchmarks, it can look like things are plateauing. Many benchmarks are saturated, and the score goes from 90 to 92 to 93. But that's mostly a property of the benchmark, not the model. Once a benchmark is close to its ceiling, it stops being informative. So the question becomes whether we're still building evaluations that track what we actually care about.

When I look at it that way, I don't think progress is slowing. It's shifting. In the pre-training era, progress was easy to see: scale up compute and data, and loss goes down along a smooth curve. That curve is still there, but the marginal gains from pre-training alone are harder to feel in daily use. The biggest jumps in the last year or two came from reinforcement learning, reasoning, and from models acting as agents: writing and running code, using tools, working on tasks over long horizons. Those are capabilities you don't really see if you only ask a model a single question and grade the answer.

So the way I'd assess it is to ask a few things. First, how long and how complex a task can the model complete reliably without a human stepping in? Is that horizon growing? I think it's growing quite fast. Second, is the model creating real economic value, doing work people would otherwise pay for, rather than just scoring well on exams? Third, is the cost of a given capability level dropping? Even if frontier capability stood still, a big drop in cost is meaningful progress.

There's also a subtler point. As models get stronger, it gets harder for people to perceive the improvement. If you ask a high school math question, last year's model and this year's model both get it right, so you feel nothing has changed. The differences show up on the hardest problems, where most users never look. So perceived slowdown and actual slowdown are different things.

Overall, I'd say the easy, visible gains from one particular recipe are slowing, but the field keeps finding new axes to scale along. The real bottleneck now is less raw model capability and more whether we can define the right tasks, environments, and evaluations to push it further. In some sense, the second half of AI is about evaluation and problem definition as much as about training.

r001.rationale: The response says saturated benchmarks approach their ceiling and then stop being informative, explaining why benchmark scores plateau even as models improve.

r002.rationale: It says improvements can be hard to perceive on easy questions and show up on harder problems, but does not state that a smaller score gain at a higher level can feel like a greater capability improvement than a larger gain at a lower level.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think "is it slowing down" is the wrong framing, or at least it's a question you can't answer without first asking: slowing down on what?

If you look at the benchmarks we used to care about, things like MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, yes, it looks like it's plateauing. But that's mostly because those benchmarks are saturated. A model scoring 95 versus 97 doesn't tell you anything. The measuring stick stopped being useful, not necessarily the models. So the first thing I'd say is that a lot of the "slowdown" narrative is an artifact of evaluation, not of capability.

The way I actually think about it is to separate two things. One is the model's raw intelligence, what it can do in a single forward pass or a single response. The other is what the model can accomplish over a long horizon when it's acting in an environment, using tools, getting feedback, correcting itself. On the first axis, I do think the gains from pure pre-training scaling have gotten more expensive. Each increment costs a lot more. But on the second axis, the agentic axis, we're very clearly not slowing down. If you measure how long a task a model can reliably complete, that's been growing something like exponentially. Two years ago a model could do a task that takes a human a few minutes. Now it's hours. That's a completely different curve from the one people are looking at when they say progress has stalled.

And the reason it's different is that the bottleneck shifted. In the first half of this whole thing, the bottleneck was the model: better architecture, more data, more compute. Now, a lot of the bottleneck is the environment and the reward. Can you build a realistic environment where the model does real work, and can you define what "doing it well" means so you can train on it? When you solve that for a domain, coding, math, you see a big jump. When you haven't solved it, customer service, research, anything where the feedback is slow and fuzzy, progress looks slow. So capability improvement now is uneven across domains, and that unevenness gets read as a slowdown by people who happen to be looking at the domains where we haven't built good environments yet.

So if someone asks me how to assess it, I'd say: don't look at static benchmarks. Look at three things. One, the horizon length of tasks the model can complete autonomously. Two, whether it can do things that have actual economic value, like close a real PR or finish a real research task end to end. Three, how fast we're able to turn a new domain into a trainable environment. If those are moving, the field is moving, regardless of what the leaderboard says.

My own view is that we're at the point where the easy, obvious gains are gone, but the harder gains are still very much there. It's less like hitting a wall and more like the terrain changed. The people who think it's slowing down are usually still driving on the old road.

r001.rationale: The response says the benchmarks are saturated and gives 95 versus 97 as an uninformative comparison, but it does not explain that approaching a 100% ceiling forces measured gains to slow.

r002.rationale: The response says a 95-to-97 benchmark change tells users little; it does not compare how score gains at higher versus lower performance levels may feel in terms of capability improvement.

astra-6.text:
I think we first need to ask what we mean by capability, and how we measure improvement. If we look at a particular benchmark and the scores are getting close to the ceiling, then improvement will naturally appear to slow down. That doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying capability is reaching a ceiling; it may mean the benchmark is no longer very informative.

I would separate a few things: the capability of the base model, the performance of a system built around that model, and the value people actually get from using it. These are related, but they don’t advance at exactly the same pace. A model might improve, yet still fall short of the reliability needed for a particular task. Conversely, better tools or a better workflow might make the same model substantially more useful.

So I’d want to look at tasks that remain difficult, hold the evaluation conditions reasonably constant, and ask: can the model solve more of them, more reliably, at the same cost? And can it handle new problems rather than just the kinds of problems represented in the benchmark?

For me, a particularly useful question is how much work the system can complete before a person has to intervene. Getting one answer right is different from carrying a task through many steps. If that ability keeps improving, I would count it as meaningful progress even if familiar benchmark scores move only a little.

So I wouldn’t infer a general slowdown from one score or from how impressive a new release feels. We need to specify which capability, under what resource constraints, and over what period.

r001.rationale: It says that as benchmark scores get close to the ceiling, improvement on that benchmark will naturally appear to slow.

r002.rationale: It distinguishes benchmark scores from usefulness, but does not say that a smaller gain at a higher performance level can feel like a greater capability improvement than a larger gain at a lower level.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we first need to ask what we mean by capability and how we’re measuring it. If you look at a particular benchmark, progress can appear to slow because the benchmark is becoming saturated. But that doesn’t necessarily mean the underlying technology has reached a limit. It may mean we need a better way to measure it.

I would separate improvements in the model itself from improvements in the system built around it. A model might get only a little better at answering a question directly, but if it can use tools, interact with an environment, and check its own work, the range of tasks it can complete could expand substantially. On the other hand, a higher benchmark score doesn’t automatically mean it can reliably do useful work.

So I’d look at whether these systems can solve harder, longer tasks with less human intervention, and at what cost. Can they recover when something goes wrong? Can they handle situations that weren’t anticipated by the person designing the test? Those are more meaningful signals to me than a single score.

There’s also a distinction between progress slowing and progress becoming more expensive. If an improvement requires much more compute, that matters economically, even if capability is still increasing. So I wouldn’t make a broad judgment from one model release or one benchmark. I’d want to look at capability, reliability, and cost together over time.

r001.rationale: The response says progress can appear to slow as a benchmark becomes saturated, but does not explain that approaching its 100% ceiling forces measured gains to slow.

r002.rationale: The response does not compare the perceived capability impact of score gains at higher versus lower benchmark performance levels.
